AppSignal
pricing should be evaluated against your application's monitored traffic, logging volume, and required retention. The smallest advertised amount is a starting point, not a reliable forecast for a Rails application with background jobs and noisy incident logs.
The EUR annual view checked on November 14, 2026 lists 250,000 monthly requests at €219 per year, or €18.25 per month when expressed as an annual-payment equivalent. The free tier lists 30,000 requests, 1GB of logs, and five-day retention. Currency and billing selections matter; this is not a USD or month-to-month quote. See the
current plans page .
Use those figures to orient the evaluation, then measure your own workload before selecting a tier.
Build a workload estimate before a price comparison
AppSignal's
pricing FAQ counts both handled client requests and background-job runs. Usage is aggregated across applications. Build the estimate from all monitored services and workers, not only the web access log. Ignoring an action changes the data you retain as well as usage, so exclude only work you genuinely do not need to investigate.

8.5% of tech job ads in Europe state the pay. Most of them only say it in the prose
# career
# regex
# typescript
# datascience
Out of 16,886 open tech jobs in Europe on 23 November 2026, 1,441 state the pay. That is 8.5%. In the United States the same count gives 49.7%, in Canada 41.9%.
The EU Pay Transparency Directive was due in national law by 7 June 2026. Most member states have not passed it yet, and the job ads show it.
I build
Sottava , a job board that reads about 2,460 companies' own hiring systems (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable and others) every hour. So these are not numbers from a job board's form. They are what the employers published themselves.
The salary field is almost always empty
The hiring systems have structured salary fields. I expected to read the pay from there and be done.
Of about 18,000 open European postings that name a technology, roughly 300 had the salary fields filled. About 1,200 more stated a range only in the description, in a sentence somewhere between the tech stack and the benefits.
So four out of five European ads that do state the pay say it only in the text. Count the fields alone and Europe looks even worse than it is.
Reading a range out of the text
A range in a posting comes in a lot of shapes:
€65,000 - €80,000 ,
65.000 – 80.000 € ,
65 000 to 80 000 EUR ,

Out of 16,886 open tech jobs in Europe on 23 November 2026, 1,441 state the pay. That is 8.5%. In the United States the same count gives 49.7%, in Canada 41.9%.
The EU Pay Transparency Directive was due in national law by 7 June 2026. Most member states have not passed it yet, and the job ads show it.
I build
Sottava , a job board that reads about 2,460 companies' own hiring systems (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable and others) every hour. So these are not numbers from a job board's form. They are what the employers published themselves.
The salary field is almost always empty
The hiring systems have structured salary fields. I expected to read the pay from there and be done.
Of about 18,000 open European postings that name a technology, roughly 300 had the salary fields filled. About 1,200 more stated a range only in the description, in a sentence somewhere between the tech stack and the benefits.
So four out of five European ads that do state the pay say it only in the text. Count the fields alone and Europe looks even worse than it is.
Reading a range out of the text
A range in a posting comes in a lot of shapes:
€65,000 - €80,000 ,
65.000 – 80.000 € ,
65 000 to 80 000 EUR ,
£85k-£111k

Out of 16,886 open tech jobs in Europe on 23 November 2026, 1,441 state the pay. That is 8.5%. In the United States the same count gives 49.7%, in Canada 41.9%.
The EU Pay Transparency Directive was due in national law by 7 June 2026. Most member states have not passed it yet, and the job ads show it.
I build
Sottava , a job board that reads about 2,460 companies' own hiring systems (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable and others) every hour. So these are not numbers from a job board's form. They are what the employers published themselves.
The salary field is almost always empty
The hiring systems have structured salary fields. I expected to read the pay from there and be done.
Of about 18,000 open European postings that name a technology, roughly 300 had the salary fields filled. About 1,200 more stated a range only in the description, in a sentence somewhere between the tech stack and the benefits.
So four out of five European ads that do state the pay say it only in the text. Count the fields alone and Europe looks even worse than it is.
Reading a range out of the text
A range in a posting comes in a lot of shapes:
€65,000 - €80,000 ,
65.000 – 80.000 € ,
65 000 to 80 000 EUR ,
£85k-£111k
the range word in several languages: to, bis, à,

Go Generics at Package Boundaries: Type Parameter Leakage, Interface Erosion, and the Constraint Design Problem
Generics in Go arrived with a specific promise: eliminate repetitive container code without sacrificing type safety. What production experience reveals is a subtler problem. The moment a generic type or function crosses a package boundary—into an SDK, a shared internal library, or a service-to-service RPC layer—its type parameters become a constraint on every consumer downstream. Get the constraint wrong and you face one of three outcomes: you break the abstraction, you force callers into type assertions they cannot safely write, or you create a proliferation of type parameter threading that makes the package graph unreadable.
This article is about that specific failure mode: how generics leak across package boundaries, what it costs operationally, and how to design constraints that remain stable under the kind of change pressure real backend services produce.

Redis lists December 1, 2026 as the end-of-life date for Redis 8.0. That's next week.
Redis 7.2 and 7.4 are older, and they're supported until December 1, 2029. Redis 6.2 is covered until April 1, 2027. So if you moved to 8.0 early to be on the current major, you're the first one who has to move again.
I'm writing this down because nothing in a cluster tells you. The image tag says
redis:8.0 , the pods are healthy, and 8 looks newer than 7.
Why 8.0 goes first
Redis Open Source has two kinds of release, and the support window depends on which kind you run. How new it is doesn't matter.
A Standard release gets security updates and critical bug fixes for 6 months after the following minor version is released. An Extended release gets them for 5 years after its own release date.
